newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Voting starts in Moldova's presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Voting starts in Moldova's presidential election.

text.p: Moldovans began voting on Sunday in the second round of the former Soviet republic's first multi- candidate presidential election, which pits President Mircea Snegur against the leftist speaker of parliament.

Snegur, 56, president since independence in 1991, took first place in the November 17 first round with 39 percent of the vote. He has been endorsed by a nationalist candidate who wants closer ties with ethnic kin in Romania.

But the president faces stiff opposition. Both the communists and Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who was knocked out in the first round, have backed parliament chairman Petru Lucinschi. Lucinschi took 28 percent of the vote two weeks ago.
Snegur has strong support in the countryside, but the deep economic crisis of the past five years has fuelled resentment.
"I'm for Lucinschi," said Valya as she swept autumn leaves from the pavement in front of her ageing single-storey house in the centre of the capital, Chisinau, early on Sunday.
"My pension's only 50 lei (about $10) a month and I don't always get it. My children don't get their wages, our two-year- old is hungry," she added. "We need a change."
Lucinschi, also 56 and like Snegur once a top Soviet communist, says Snegur might use police to help him influence the voting, which is being oberved by international monitors.

Last March, Snegur tried to sack the defence minister for corruption but Sangheli opposed him, causing a menacing split in the army. The constitutional court ruled against Snegur, who plans to sack Sangheli's government if he wins on Sunday.

There was no sign of unusual security or tension in central Chisinau as polls opened at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT). Police said Snegur's supporters would rally at the government building at midday, although campaigning is banned on election day.
The president remains popular with many of Moldova's 4.3 million people, despite their economic troubles.
"I'm voting for Snegur. He gave us our independence, he knows what to do," said Glavia, a Chisinau housewife in her 40s. "The problem is the government does not let him do what he needs to."

Snegur has pledged to press on with market reforms -- but wants greater presidential powers to do it. He dismisses fears among the one-third Russian-speaking minority that closer ties with Bucharest could lead to union. Soviet dictator Josef Stalin carved Moldova from mainly Romanian territory in World War Two.
Lucinschi, a wiry intellectual who presents himself as a social democrat, accuses Snegur of seeking vast powers.
Backed by state television, the speaker has played on what he says was Snegur's role in the conflict with Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking separatists east of the Dnestr river in 1992.

The region, with a population of 700,000, broke away in 1990, fearing Romanian domination. Dnestr, still garrisoned by Russian peacekeeping troops, was not voting on Sunday, although some residents may vote in other parts of Moldova.
Lucinschi also reminds Moldovans they depend on Russia for their energy -- for which they are finding it hard to pay.
Early voting was slack at the city's Middle School No 37.
The first man to retreat into a curtained booth to mark his cross and drop the paper in the box voted for the president.
"I'm an adviser to Snegur," he explained with a smile.
Some 2.7 million electors have until 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) to vote. A preliminary result is expected after midnight.
